title: Selection of Textiles and Clothing
summary: Fibre properties influence choice: length and appearance (staple fibres such as cotton, jute and wool give a rough look and get dirty easily; filament fibres such as silk, nylon and polyester give a smooth shiny look and stay clean; starch gives only a temporary smoothness), moisture absorption (cotton absorbs perspiration and keeps the skin cool, so is best for summers, undergarments and baby clothes; synthetics absorb little and are uncomfortable in summer), heat conductivity (cotton and rayon are good conductors and keep the body cool; silk and synthetics are poor conductors; wool is a very bad conductor and keeps the body warm, so is best for winter) and strength (wool, silk and rayon become weak when wet; cotton and synthetics are strong when wet and can be scrubbed; use them for daily wear; nylon is strongest and is used for parachutes and ropes; silk for occasional use). Construction: knitting gives stretch (socks, undergarments, sweaters); weaving gives smooth, firm fabric for dresses. Finishes: shrinkage-control saves buying extra cloth, waterproofing for umbrellas; an over-starched cloth hides poor quality (rub the corner: white powder means avoid).

Climate (cotton in summer, wool in winter; turbans and long robes in deserts), occasion (bright dresses for weddings; simple formal clothes for an interview; comfortable fit for routine days), age (infants: soft, light, absorbent cotton, simple to put on, front openings with snaps; school children: strong, durable, easy to launder, extra seam allowance; teenagers: fit, style and mix-and-match for variety; adults: easy-care, wrinkle-free clothes for working women; old age: light, loose, front-opening clothes with large buttons) and profession or activity (doctors and nurses in white; uniforms; sportsmen in absorbent shorts; travelling clothes dark and not crumpling; overalls, mining suits, wet suits, space suits and fireproof clothing; snug cotton in the kitchen, not hanging dupattas).

A label (paper, plastic or tag attached to a product) gives information; a marking is printed on the surface of fabric or 'thaan'. Types: brand labels (company identity), descriptive labels (size, variety), certification labels (Woolmark for pure wool), care labels (washing, ironing, storing) and informative labels (composition, performance, care and use). Malpractices: giving less quantity or poor quality (short measuring rod, stretching fabric: 4 m turns out to be 3.8 m), cheating on price (charging more than the printed price or adding taxes), selling defective goods (seconds sold as fresh) and giving false, misleading or incomplete labels. The Consumer Protection Regulation Act (1988) covers these. Be alert: watch the measuring, check the printed price, read labels and use the Act.
## Judging quality of fabrics and garments

Material: pleasing to touch; durability depends on fibre, yarn strength, twist and compact construction (closely woven fabric is stronger and more serviceable). Weave: avoid long floats (they snag), test strength by tension between thumbs, filler yarns should meet the selvedge at right angles (an oblique angle means off-grain) and the weave should be uniform when held to the light. Finish: smell should be clean and not oily, dyeing even (colour rubbed off along creases means poor dye), geometric patterns meeting the selvedge at right angles, no powdery dust when rubbed (too much starch or gum hides poor quality), and dense, fine pile in velvets and towels. Ready-made garments: design (style line, shape, colour, texture), fit (shoulders, bust, waist, length; not undersized or oversized), workmanship (look at the wrong side, double and finished seams, no puckers, enough seam allowance, working fasteners and zips, well-defined collar edges, neat piping and facings), price (matches quality; high price is not always high quality) and care and maintenance (read care labels; choose minimum care; check colour fastness).

objective: Complete the table by selecting the appropriate fabric for each end use and giving one reason. Choose from cotton, nylon, wool, silk. End uses: summer clothing; winter sweater.
Summer clothing: cotton, because it absorbs perspiration and conducts heat away. Winter sweater: wool, because it is a bad conductor of heat and keeps the body warm.
State whether True or False and correct the false one. (a) Synthetic fibres are ideal for baby's undergarments. (b) Doctors wear white coats to look fashionable.
(a) False: synthetics are non-absorbent; cotton is ideal. (b) False: white looks clean and protects against infection.
Match Column I with Column II. I: (1) Baby garments (2) Teenagers (3) School-going children. II: (a) Variety to mix and match (b) Strong and durable (c) Absorbent cotton.

Justify. (a) A closely woven fabric is more serviceable. (b) Long floats in a weave should be avoided.
(a) It has more yarns so it is stronger. (b) Long floats snag easily and weaken the fabric.
vsa: What will you check in seams and fasteners while purchasing ready-made garments?
Check that seams are double, finished, free of puckers and have enough allowance. Open and close fasteners and zips to see that they work well.
What is the difference between a label and a marking?
A label is a piece of paper, plastic or tag attached to a garment with information. A marking is printed on the surface of fabric or 'thaan' for identification.
What three points would you check to ensure buying good quality fabric?
Check that the cloth is pleasing to touch and closely and evenly woven. Check for even dyeing with no powdery dust and a clean smell.
Which three characteristics would you consider while buying clothes for summers?
The fabric should be absorbent like cotton. It should be light, loose and light-coloured and easy to launder.

or: Which three characteristics would you consider while buying clothes for your college-going sister?
Fit and style that she likes, a mix-and-match combination for variety, and easy care and colour fastness.

vsa: Why is cotton preferred for summer wear?
Cotton absorbs perspiration and is a good conductor of heat. It keeps the body cool.
List any two malpractices in selling fabrics.
Giving less quantity by stretching the fabric or using a short rod. Selling seconds as fresh goods or giving misleading labels.
sa: Explain the importance of labels and markings on textile products. How do they help consumers make informed decisions?

(i) Labels and markings give information on fibre content, brand, size and care. (ii) Care labels tell washing and ironing instructions and certification labels show standards such as the Woolmark. (iii) This helps consumers judge quality, avoid misleading goods and choose suitable clothes.
What are the different malpractices prevalent in selling fabrics?

(i) Giving lesser quantity or poor quality by stretching the fabric. (ii) Cheating on price by charging more than the printed price. (iii) Selling defective goods as fresh and giving false or incomplete labels.
How will you judge the quality of a fabric? (three points)

(i) Material and weave: pleasing to touch, closely and uniformly woven, no long floats. (ii) Finish: even dyeing, clean smell and no powder when rubbed. (iii) Check that yarns meet the selvedge at right angles and patterns are matched.
Explain how care and maintenance and price affect the choice of ready-made garments (three points).
(i) Read the care label before buying. (ii) Choose fabric that needs minimum care and has fast colour. (iii) Price should match the quality and wear, since a high price is not always high quality.
la: Discuss the factors that influence the selection of clothing for different age groups, with examples for each age group.

(i) Infants need soft, light, absorbent cotton clothes with simple openings. (ii) School-going children need strong, durable, easy-to-launder clothes with extra seam allowance. (iii) Teenagers want fit and style and mix-and-match clothes for variety, such as a few salwars with several kameez or jeans with T-shirts. (iv) Adults, especially working women, need easy-care, wrinkle-free clothes. (v) Old people need light, loose clothes with front openings and large buttons. (vi) Climate, occasion and profession also influence selection.
